newsitem.title: ITALY: THE PROTEUS COLUMN- Italian insurance market, WIN.
newsitem.headline: THE PROTEUS COLUMN- Italian insurance market, WIN.

text.p: Executive board members from Swiss Re together with those from Uniorias will meet with key clients from the Italian market in Rome on Friday to give a presentation about traditional reinsurance and alternative risk transfer.
The meeting comes as Swiss Re nears completion of its restructuring of operations in Italy following the acquisition of 49 percent of Uniorias in February.
It is a further sign that Swiss Re sees Italy as the next major European market for the insurers and reinsurers.

It is perhaps no coincidence then that French company Scor announced on Monday it is also reorganising its Italian activities and will transfer both life and non-life activities to its subsidiary Vittoria Riassicurazioni.

Meanwhile in the primary insurance market, Italy's Generali is looking outwards. At its AGM last week chairman Antoine Bernheim said he was not happy with Generali's 3.5 per cent share of the French market, and indicated he was looking at acquisitions. Targets were not identified. GAN was ruled out, but no clear indications were given on the question of interest in Athena. Market rumours linking the two have been gaining momentum in recent weeks, and Athena's owners, the Worms group, have done nothing to quash suggestions they would welcome a sale. Generali is also understood to be seeking expansion in Spain.

Today sees the launch of the much-vaunted World Insurance Network(WIN). The concept is that it will lead the way to electronic trading of insurance and save the industry billions in costs. In reality it has several problems to overcome. One is the reluctance of many insurers and reinsurers and brokers, particularly in Europe, to move their business on to desktop computers which they lack skills in using. Another is uncertainty about whether the system should be run by the big four (formerly the big six) broking companies, partly because they have no experience of running such systems and partly because of a suggestion of clash of interests.
There are also growing indications that the commitment of J&H Marsh McLennan, currently the world's biggest broker, to WIN is waning and that it is preparing to do its own thing.
WIN's organisers have always said that today's launch will not be a big bang. They will not want it to be a damp squib either.
